This page is the interactive version of the lesson notes (PDF). Each section
starts with a question in a game studio. Then it explains the idea behind
it. It ends with a **Do it** task and one set of questions. The full
explanations, examples and exercises are in the notes.

## Key terms

{{< glossary premise protagonist conflict stakes setting inciting-incident core-mechanic pitch >}}

## 6.1 The story in two sentences: the premise

- A **premise** says the story in one or two sentences: who the character
  is, what the character wants, what stands in the way and what is at
  stake.
- Template: *When* [inciting incident], [character] *must* [goal]
  *before / or* [stakes], *but* [obstacle].
- *Moon Diver*: "When the base on the Moon starts to lose power, Pip, a
  small diving robot, must find the lost crystals in the Deep Lake before
  the lights go out for good, but ice eels and dark water stand in the way."
- A premise stops at the conflict. It does not tell the ending.

![The parts of a premise.](images/premise-parts.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
A premise is not a summary of every stage. The listener must want to know
how it ends.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The premise of a game you know"}
Choose a mobile game with a story. Find its inciting incident, character,
goal, stakes and obstacle. Write its premise with the template.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Parts of a premise"}
The premise: "When the dragon steals the village bell, Tala, a young
shepherd, must bring it back before the winter festival, but the mountain
path is full of traps." Choose the part. You can use an answer more than
once.

::: {.match extra="the setting"}
"the dragon steals the village bell"
:   the inciting incident

"Tala, a young shepherd"
:   the character

"bring it back"
:   the goal

"before the winter festival"
:   the stakes

"the mountain path is full of traps"
:   the obstacle
:::
:::

## 6.2 From premise to play

- In a game, the player **acts**. What does the player do again and again?
  That is the **core mechanic**: dive, run, slide, sort, build.
- A good premise already shows the core mechanic. The goal and the obstacle
  need this action.
- A desert courier before sunset: run, jump, slide (one run: 1 minute). A
  boat driver in a flooded city: slide blocks (one level: 3 minutes).
- "A story about friendship and hope": no character, no goal, no danger,
  no gameplay.

![A good premise already says what the player does.](images/premise-play.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
"A detective remembers her childhood" may be a good film. But what does the
player do?
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the core mechanic"}
For your premise from 6.1, write the core mechanic in two or three verbs.
Does the goal need this action? Does one round fit a few minutes?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · The play in the premise"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="read long texts|nothing is missing"}
"A courier must cross the desert before sunset, but a sandstorm buries the road." What does the player do?
:   run, jump and slide

"A boat driver must lead the families to the hill, but floating cars block the streets." What does the player do?
:   slide the blocks to open a path

"A story about friendship and hope." What is missing?
:   a character, a goal, a danger and the play

What do we call the action that the player repeats again and again?
:   the core mechanic

Which premise fits a one-minute runner?
:   a courier racing a sandstorm to a village
:::
:::

## 6.3 Test and improve a premise

- Test a draft with six questions: **Who?** **What goal?** **What stands
  in the way?** **What is at stake?** **Where?** **What does the player
  do?**
- Each "no" shows what to add.
- Keep it short: about 25 to 40 words. Use specific words: "Adam, a young
  fisherman", not "a boy"; "before dawn", not "soon".
- Draft: "A boy lives in a city by the sea and has adventures." Better:
  "When a storm sinks the ferry, Adam, a young fisherman, must bring the
  medicine to the island before dawn, but the sea is full of wreckage. The
  player steers the boat between the wrecks."

![The six questions on a weak draft and on a better version.](images/premise-check.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
"Or something bad happens" is vague. Concrete stakes make the player care.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/premise-doctor.html" poster="sims/premise-doctor.png" title="Premise Doctor: what is missing?" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Premise Doctor"}
In **Premise Doctor**, find the missing parts of the five drafts. Then test
your own premise with the six questions and improve it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · What is missing?"}
Choose what is missing from each draft.

::: {.match extra="the character"}
"A boy lives in a city by the sea and has adventures."
:   the goal, the obstacle, the stakes and the play

"Nour must lead the families to the hill, but floating cars block the streets. The player slides blocks."
:   the stakes

"Lina must make her grandmother's farm grow again before the spring market, or the family must sell it, but the soil is dry."
:   the player's action

"…or something bad happens." What is wrong with these stakes?
:   they are vague

About how long is a good premise?
:   25 to 40 words
:::
:::

## Game challenge: the Night Owl pitch {.challenge}

Work alone. Use every section of today.

The producer of *Night Owl Games* gives a brief: **a mobile puzzle game;
levels of 3 minutes; a flooded city; the player slides blocks to open a
path.** Build a premise that fits it, from cards: an inciting incident, a
character, a goal, the stakes, an obstacle and the player's action.

{{< sim file="sims/pitch-room.html" poster="sims/pitch-room.png" title="Pitch Room: build a premise that fits the brief" kind="game" height="760" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Fit the brief"}
The brief: a puzzle game, levels of 3 minutes, a flooded city, the player
slides blocks. Choose the card that fits.

::: {.match extra="When aliens land on the Moon"}
Which inciting incident fits?
:   When the river floods the old city

Which character fits?
:   Nour, a young boat driver

Which player action fits?
:   slide the blocks to open a path

Which stakes are concrete?
:   the families stay on the rooftops all night
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · Why not? (harder)"}
The same brief. The producer rejects some cards. Choose the reason.

::: {.match extra="it is too short"}
"but a dragon attacks from the sky"
:   it does not fit the sliding puzzles

"the city" as the character
:   a place is not a character

"must win a car race"
:   the goal does not fit a puzzle game about a flood

"The player shoots enemies."
:   the brief asks for sliding blocks

"or something bad happens"
:   the stakes are not clear
:::
:::

## Summary {.summary}

- A premise says who wants what, what stands in the way and what is at stake.
- Template: When…, [character] must [goal] before/or [stakes], but [obstacle].
- A game premise also shows the core mechanic: what the player does again and again.
- Test it with six questions: who, goal, obstacle, stakes, where, play.
- Keep it short and specific; make the stakes concrete.
